questions.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{12}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))^{2}+(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(6\theta )+36{sin}^{2}⁡(6\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\theta {e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta {e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={e}^{\theta }+\theta {e}^{\theta }=(1+\theta ){e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\theta {e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{((1+\theta ){e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}{e}^{2\theta }+(1+2\theta +{\theta }^{2}){e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1){e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\theta }\sqrt{2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{e}^{\theta }.

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(3{e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{(3{e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{e}^{2\theta }+9{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{18{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /4}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =3\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Find the arc length $L$ of the polar curve $r={3}^{\theta /4}$ for $0\le \theta \le 4.$ Do not round the answer.

$L=$
{{field-1}}$\sqrt{{ln}^{2}⁡3+16}$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={3}^{\theta /4},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={3}^{\theta /4}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{{({3}^{\theta /4})}^{2}+{({3}^{\theta /4}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{{3}^{\theta /2}+{3}^{\theta /2}\cdot \frac{{ln}^{2}⁡3}{16}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{(1+\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡3}{16}){3}^{\theta /2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡3}{16}}{\int }_{0}^{4}{3}^{\theta /4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡3}{16}}\cdot \frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot {3}^{\theta /4}\,{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡3}{16}}\cdot \frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\cdot ({3}^{1}-{3}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡3}{16}}\cdot \frac{8}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\sqrt{{ln}^{2}⁡3+16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{5\pi }{6}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above).
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}1\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\theta {|}_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =2(\frac{5\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the polar curve $r=3-\sin(7\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi,$ shown in blue in the diagram above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=3-\sin(7\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} =-7\cos(7\theta)
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(3-\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}+(-7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+49{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+1+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{10-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2(1-\cos\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ (shown in blue in the picture above).
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1-\cos\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\sin\theta.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now use the half-angle formula $1-\cos\theta =2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={-4\cdot 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
